With Red Hat OpenShift Lightspeed 2 on Red Hat OpenShift 5, you can configure autonomous agents to start troubleshooting when a cluster alert fires. An agent can inspect cluster resources, read logs and events, and propose a fix. With the required approvals, the workflow can then apply the fix and verify the result.

In this article, you'll learn how this workflow works, how to enable it, and how to control its level of automation. We'll then test it with a cluster failure, following the investigation from the initial alert to remediation and verification.

OpenShift Lightspeed autonomous agents follow a workflow with 4 tasks: analyzing the problem, applying a fix, checking the result, and escalating when you need further help. You can use the same agent across stages or configure different agents for each one.

The process starts when OpenShift Lightspeed detects a firing alert that matches its configuration. It creates an AgenticRun, a custom resource that tracks the investigation and its progress through the workflow:

An approval policy controls whether each stage requires manual approval or starts automatically. By default, every stage waits for approval. Later in this article, we'll configure a policy that lets analysis and verification run automatically while keeping execution under your control.

Figure 1 shows an example of an AgenticRun in the Red Hat OpenShift web console after the agent diagnoses an alert and executes a fix.

OpenShift Lightspeed autonomous agents are available as a Technology Preview. Red Hat doesn't support Technology Preview features with production service level agreements (SLAs), and they might not be functionally complete. Red Hat doesn't recommend using them in production. These features provide early access to upcoming product features, enabling customers to test functionality and provide feedback during the development process.

For details, see Technology Preview Features Support Scope.

In the Red Hat OpenShift web console, go to Ecosystem → Software Catalog and search for OpenShift Lightspeed, as shown in Figure 2. Accept the default settings, and select Install.

Installing the operator prepares the controllers. We'll configure alert filtering next, then create the OLSConfig custom resource that deploys the Lightspeed services.

By default, no alerts trigger an automatic investigation. To enable this behavior, configure the alerts-adapter-config ConfigMap and specify which Alertmanager receivers the agents should monitor.

Alertmanager uses routing rules to assign alerts to named receivers based on labels such as severity or namespace. By listing receiver names under allowedReceivers, you reuse those rules to select which alerts can trigger an investigation. This example allows alerts routed to the Critical receiver:

Critical is a receiver name, rather than a severity label. The default OpenShift Alertmanager configuration routes alerts with severity: critical to this receiver. If your cluster uses different routing rules, adjust the receiver name accordingly.

The tools.skills section shows how to add optional skills to guide the agent during analysis. This example uses the cluster-troubleshoot skill from the openshift/agentic-skills repository, packaged as an Open Container Initiative (OCI) image and published at quay.io/openshiftanalytics/agentic-skills.

In the next step, we'll reference this ConfigMap in the OLSConfig to enable alert processing. For more configuration options, see Autonomous agentic troubleshooting.

The alert configuration is now in place. Next, we'll create the OLSConfig that deploys the Lightspeed services and connects them to this configuration.

OpenShift Lightspeed intelligent assistant and OpenShift Lightspeed autonomous agents currently use separate LLM credential configurations. We'll configure the credentials for intelligent assistant here, then configure those for autonomous agents in the next step.

Now create the OLSConfig with the alerts adapter enabled:

Wait for the app server to become available. The initial image downloads can take several minutes:

OpenShift Lightspeed autonomous agents require an LLM provider and a model. The following configuration creates the provider credentials, connects them through an LLMProvider, and defines the default agent used by the workflow:

The workflow uses the default agent unless you select another agent. You can define additional Agent resources to use different models or settings for specific stages.

The agent now has a model, but it also needs access to cluster data. We'll grant read access for investigation and give the controller permissions to create remediation sandboxes.

The agent service account needs cluster-wide read access. The operator doesn't create these bindings automatically. Keep lightspeed-agent in the subjects of both bindings: the controller uses this account to find the reader bindings and grant read permissions to sandbox service accounts. Without the reader binding, analysis fails before the agent starts, with an error such as "no ClusterRoleBinding found with subject openshift-lightspeed/lightspeed-agent." Apply both bindings before starting an AgenticRun:

For this walkthrough, we grant the controller cluster-admin access so it can create the roles that remediation sandboxes need. Each sandbox receives the permissions defined for its task:

For a more restricted setup, limit the controller permissions to the operations you intend to allow. The controller permissions and the permissions assigned to each temporary sandbox are separate parts of the access model.

With credentials and permissions in place, we can decide where the workflow should pause for review. Without an ApprovalPolicy, every stage waits for manual approval.

For this example, we'll let analysis, verification, and escalation run automatically. Execution will still require your approval, so you can review the diagnosis and proposed changes before the agent applies them:

Approval is at the stage level: you approve or reject an entire stage, not individual commands within it. With this policy, only execution pauses for your sign-off.

The configuration is complete. We'll now deploy an application with an incorrect image name and follow the workflow through investigation, approval, and verification.

The image name origin-ehllo-openshift is a typo—the correct name is origin-hello-openshift. The pods enter ImagePullBackOff, and the WebServerImagePullFailure alert fires after the condition has remained true for 1 minute, plus evaluation
